 Some big news over the weekend. The leader of one of the world’s most valuable companies has potentially found himself at the center of an international spy campaign. It’s a saga that could upend not just the AI trade, but the entire economy. (And cause people in Silicon Valley to second-guess their romantic partners.)  
 Nvidia’s board of directors said Sunday it’s investigating whether CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a " foreign intelligence effort ."  
 Earlier in the day, Huang sent a message to staff admitting he had been "unfaithful" to his wife, Lori .  
 "My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," Huang wrote. "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully." 
 You can read Huang’s full note to Nvidia workers here . 
 The market responded: Nvidia shares were 4.5% lower in premarket trading Monday , a move that would erase about $190 billion from Friday’s valuation. 
 The New York Times reported last month that US officials believe Alice Huang, who has been an executive for Megaspeed,  was a Chinese intelligence asset passing information to Beijing. The outlet reported that surveillance of Alice Huang showed that she had developed a relationship with the Nvidia founder. 
 At the time, an Nvidia spokesperson told the Times that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual or unexpected.” The CEO also previously told Bloomberg his relationship with Alice Huang was “ all completely normal and not unusual .” 
 Trump has already backed Huang , calling him an “honorable guy” and saying he should remain CEO.  
 The seriousness of the investigation isn’t just due to the size and central role Nvidia plays in the AI industry. Jensen Huang is viewed as one of the faces of AI, and his hands-on management style , with dozens of direct reports , means he plays a crucial role in Nvidia’s day-to-day operations. 
 Here’s what industry experts are saying about Nvidia’s investigation into its CEO.

 Business Insider, this matters beyond the politics. When servicers get the billing wrong, charge interest that should not be there, or lose count of payments toward forgiveness, the borrower who catches it is the one who kept their own records. Hearings may fix the system one day. In the meantime, every household with a loan should know three things cold. What they owe. What they have actually paid. And who to call when the numbers do not match. That is the defense a family can play today.
